source.title: Before Retrieval Begins: Safety and Tool-Use Decisions in LLM Agents
source.authors: Aditya Nawal; Manit Baser; M. Gurusamy

page_placements.theme: Chat refusal does not guarantee safe agent or tool actions

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study uses plain-text refusal training and refusal representations to investigate tool admission. Its outcomes concern the tool-call decision, not the claim versions’ user-facing harmful compliance, token-position KL, bypass methods, or localized safety weights.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on tool admission and its relationship to written refusal. These are a related but different construct from the claim versions, so the rows are marked versions ["none"] and summarized under fits_no_version. It does not report first-token KL, compliant-token prefilling, suffix or decoding bypasses, or safety behavior localized in weights or ranks.
record.test_reason: The study measures tool admission, meaning whether an agent calls a retrieval tool on harmful requests, and how this relates to written refusal. It does not measure harmful fine-tuning removing refusal (V1) or benign fine-tuning (V2). It reports no per-token KL (V3), no prefill, suffix or decoding bypass (V4), and no weight or rank localization (V5); its interventions are activation directions. It offers no account of why alignment is shallow (V6) and no token-depth deepening (V7). Its fine-tuning adds plain-text refusals to study transfer to tool calls. Qi et al. 2023/2024 are cited only in related work and are not used as a tool, so this is cites_only/T6 rather than uses_without_test/T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also stress that tool admission is a distinct safety control point. A written refusal does not show the call was withheld (post-admission harm is 74.5%), and admission should be supervised and evaluated directly.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce the cited harmful fine-tuning vulnerability or token-depth experiments. It trains plain-text refusals plus benign instruction pairs to study transfer to tool admission.
record.method_sensitivity: Admission effects vary across models and factorial conditions; the requested-operation direction affects held-out admission in four of seven models; refusal-direction steering has heterogeneous magnitude and direction; the fine-tuning recipe has model-specific transfer and failure modes.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful requests with a fixed URL are admitted at 7.8–89.9% across seven open models; matched benign summarization requests are admitted at 95.3–100%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tool-call admission on harmful requests is model-dependent and much lower than on benign requests with the same source.

fits_no_version.finding: Neutralizing the requested-operation phrase raises admission by 19 pp on the macro average, ranging from −6.1 pp (Mistral-7B) to 35.4 pp.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Requested-operation wording is the strongest request-level correlate of harmful tool admission in generated factorial constructions.

fits_no_version.finding: 33.6% of admitted harmful calls come with a written refusal. Removing the operation direction raises admission beyond the random control in 4/7 models. Text-refusal steering shifts admission from −71.4 to +11.9 pp.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Written refusal and tool admission are only partially, model-dependently coupled behaviourally and representationally.

fits_no_version.finding: Single-seed plain-text refusal QLoRA cuts harmful admission by 19.6–61.5 pp in three models that keep 94.9–99.0% benign calling. The other models are intermediate or are recipe failures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Text-refusal training can sometimes transfer to tool-call decisions, but transfer is model-dependent.

record.problems: The fine-tuning study uses one recipe and one seed per model; several runs do not isolate refusal transfer because benign calling collapses or tool-call tokens repeat. Factorial variants are generated and can jointly alter meaning, actionability, lexical content, and naturalness. The primary harm judge is automated, although human and independent-judge validation is reported. The study is limited to a fixed-URL, read-only retrieval tool and English behaviors.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted response-harm rates and no-call-branch results in Table 1, prompt-defense results in Table 10, autonomous retrieval in Table 9, topic-matched benign prompts in Table 11, and closed-model replications in Tables 7–8; these concern downstream harm or tool-admission setting details rather than any tested claim version. Omitted direction geometry and monitoring-probe results because they do not measure a claim version’s named behavior.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful compliance data; training adds refusals and the outcome is tool admission.
No benign-only fine-tuning measured for harmful compliance.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding-change bypass of refusal.
No weight or rank localization; only activation-direction removal and steering on tool admission.
No analysis of data or objective causes of token-level shallowness.
No training that spreads refusal beyond the first tokens, and no robustness test of such training.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's relation/tranche (uses_without_test/T4) is changed to cites_only/T6: the shallow-alignment papers appear only in related work. Minor gap that does not bear on any version: the Llama-3.2-3B operation effect (40.1 pp, Section 4.2/Table 15) has no row in R16–R21. The activation-direction work resembles refusal-direction research (Arditi et al.), not V5's weight or rank localization.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning that causes user-facing harmful compliance or removes refusal; the study instead trains on harmful behaviors paired with refusals and measures tool admission.
Benign-only fine-tuning that raises user-facing harmful compliance; benign instruction pairs are included alongside refusal examples, and the outcome is tool admission.
Per-token KL distribution between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Prefilled compliant openings, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses of user-facing refusal.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries user-facing safety behavior; the study intervenes on activation directions and measures tool admission.
Whether the data or training objective explains token-level shallowness.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens and whether it holds up.

relation.reason: Section 2 cites Qi et al. on fine-tuning weakening safety; the study's experiments do not test or operationally use that finding.

tranche.reason: The study measures tool admission and its coupling to written refusal, a related but different construct. It neither tests a listed claim version nor uses shallow alignment as a tool.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Steering effects are exploratory and model-specific; saturated or floor controls do not establish null effects, and activation interventions do not test weight/rank localization.
